metadata.title: Adults with Low Proficiency in Literacy or Numeracy (EN)

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: This OECD working paper uses microdata from the OECD 2012 Survey of Adult Skills (PIAAC) to describe and compare adults with low literacy and/or numeracy proficiency and to relate proficiency and skill use to social and economic outcomes. The report does not provide the specific PIAAC sampling/replicate weight variables (e.g., student design weights or BRR/jackknife) in the excerpted text, so the exact weighting implementation cannot be confirmed from the provided material. The analysis is based on proficiency levels (e.g., Level 1 or below) and on derived measures of engagement in reading, writing and numeracy practices, as well as reading component task performance (print vocabulary, sentence processing, passage comprehension) and participation in adult education and training. Analysts using the underlying PIAAC data should apply the complex survey design weights supplied with PIAAC to obtain population-representative estimates and correct standard errors; however, this paper’s excerpt does not document the specific weight variable names or whether weights were explicitly applied in each chapter.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The paper’s excerpted content focuses on proficiency levels (e.g., Level 1 or below) and on reading component task performance and engagement/participation outcomes, but it does not document how missing data were handled in the analytic workflow. Because the provided text does not specify an imputation or deletion rule (e.g., complete-case, multiple imputation), the missing-data strategy cannot be verified from the excerpt. This is therefore treated as a reporting gap for missing-data handling rather than a design feature of a non-cognitive DV.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used OECD 2012 Survey of Adult Skills (PIAAC) data to define 'low proficiency' adults as those scoring at Level 1 or below in literacy and/or numeracy, and then compared them to higher-proficiency groups (notably Levels 4 and 5) across demographic/socio-economic characteristics, skill-use engagement, reading component performance, and participation in adult education and training. The excerpt does not specify additional analytic restrictions (e.g., specific age bands, paper-based vs computer-based subsamples, or complete-case rules), so the filtering criteria beyond the Level 1 definition cannot be further detailed from the provided text.

data.outcome_summary: This OECD Education Working Paper synthesizes and analyzes OECD 2012 Survey of Adult Skills (PIAAC) information to characterize adults with low literacy and/or numeracy proficiency and to examine how proficiency relates to engagement in reading, writing and numeracy practices, social/economic outcomes, basic reading component skills, and participation in adult education and training. “Low proficiency” is defined as scoring at Level 1 or below on PIAAC literacy or numeracy scales (with an estimated proficiency score threshold of less than 226). Across participating OECD countries, the paper reports that 12.3% of adults score at or below Level 1 in both literacy and numeracy, with additional shares scoring at or below Level 1 in only one domain. It finds that engagement in literacy practices is strongly associated with many outcomes and that low-proficiency adults participate less in adult education and training, with much of the participation gap explained by socio-demographic and employment characteristics. The excerpt does not report ML model performance metrics or document PV/missing-data handling procedures, so the results should be interpreted as descriptive and regression-based associations rather than as validated predictive ML evidence.
